'''''Zingiber spectabile''''' is a species of [[Zingiber|true ginger]], native to [[Maritime Southeast Asia]].  It is primarily grown in the West as an ornamental plant,<ref>{{cite book|last=Forsyth|first=Holly|title=The Constant Gardener|year=2007|publisher=Miegunyah Press|isbn=9780522854329|page=100}}</ref> although it has been used in [[South-East Asia]] as a medicinal herb.<ref name="Wiart">{{cite book|last=Wiart|first=Christophe|title=Medicinal Plants of China, Korea, and Japan|year=2012|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781439899113|pages=70–71}}</ref>

==Name==
The scientific name of the species is ''Zingiber spectabile''.  "Zingiber" is originally from a [[Sanskrit]] word that means "shaped like a horn" and refers to the horn-shaped leaves of most species of ginger.  "Spectabile" is derived from the [[Latin]] ''spectabilis'', meaning 'visible' or 'spectacular'.<ref name="simpson" />

The plant is commonly known in the West by the common name "beehive ginger", due to its unusual [[inflorescence]]s which resemble a [[Beehive#Skeps|skep beehive]].<ref name="simpson">{{cite web|title=Zingiber spectabile Griff.|url=http://www.somemagneticislandplants.com.au/index.php/plants/24-zingiber-spectabile|last=Simpson|first=Donald|access-date=2 November 2013}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>  It is also referred to by the common names "Ginger wort" or "Malaysian ginger".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.herbcyclopedia.com/index.php?option=com_zoo&task=item&item_id=397&Itemid=193|title=Zingiber spectabile (Beehive ginger)|publisher=Herbcyclopedia|access-date=2 November 2013}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Maraca_-_Ginger_shampoo_(Zingiber_spectabile)_(14681772670).jpg|thumb|''Zingiber spectabile'']]

In common with most plants in genus ''Zingiber'', the leaves of the plant are long and mostly oblong shaped, tapering to a single point at their tip.  Under ideal circumstances, the plant can reach a height of {{convert|4.5|m|ft}}, or even more.<ref name="chee" />

The plant's inflorescence is set atop a spike and can measure up to {{convert|30|cm|in}} in height.  The bracts attached to the structure can differ in colour, from white, to yellow, orange, or even red, often darkening as the bracts mature and develop.<ref name="simpson" />  The flowers themselves are small, with purple petals and yellow spots, and a fragile, papery texture.<ref name="chee" />

==Uses==
In [[Indonesia]], the plant has been used in [[traditional medicine]]<ref name="weiss">{{cite book|last=Weiss|first=E. A.|title=Spice Crops|year=2002|publisher=CABI|isbn=9780851996059|page=338}}</ref> to treat inflammation of the eyes.<ref name="Wiart" />  It is prepared for use by pounding the leaves of the plant into a thick paste, and then topically applying it to the required part of the body.  It has also been recorded being used to treat [[burn]]s, as a treatment for headaches and back pain, and as an agent for [[food preservation]].<ref name="chee">{{cite journal|last=Chee|first=Beng Jin|title=The Spectacular Ginger: Zingiber spectabile|publisher=Malaysian Naturalist|volume=September 2010|pages=12–13}}</ref>

Academic research has found that the plant has [[antimicrobial]] properties,<ref name="dubey">{{cite book|last=Dubey|first=N. K.|title=Natural Products in Plant Pest Management|year=2011|publisher=CABI|page=69}}</ref> and significant concentrations of the [[Zerumbone synthase]] [[enzyme]], which may be effective in treating [[colon cancer]].<ref name="sadhu">{{cite journal|last=Sadhu|first=Samir Kumar|author2=Amina Khatun |author3=Takashi Ohtsuki |author4=Masami Ishibashi |year=2007|title=First isolation of sesquiterpenes and flavonoids from Zingiber spectabile and identification of zerumbone as the major cell growth inhibitory component|journal=Natural Product Research|volume=21|issue=14|pages=1242–1247|issn=1478-6419|doi=10.1080/14786410701371421|pmid=18075886|s2cid=32918590}}</ref>
